analysis.title: International Market Intelligence | Morning Briefing (October 28, 2026)
key_insights: Asia is mostly higher with tech and AI leading. SK Hynix's results, its shareholder return messaging and its expectation that the memory shortage lasts through 2030 drove a sharp risk-on move in the memory trade.

Recent AI financing announcements make it less likely that capex is cut materially for lack of funding. JPM sees room for a bounce in AI infrastructure because the theme is oversold (the SOX/SPX drawdown rivals 2008) and fundamentals remain intact.

No geopolitical breakthrough. WSJ headlines flag possible US vs Iran escalation after the midterms. Russia vs Ukraine peace talks have revived, but the author's geopolitical indicators only ticked higher.
Gold holding around $4,000/oz is a good sign, but the author doubts it is an equity hedge because its rolling correlation to equities is quite high.
Israel's elections are projected to be inconclusive, with a period of dealmaking to form a coalition expected.

UK Budget expected to do no harm. JPM expects the 2026/27 deficit revised up to £124bn (3.8% of GDP), small targeted tax rises of about £5bn and headroom near £20bn. Watch items are a banks tax, housebuilding, gambling and business rates relief for leisure and retail.

Gilt impact expected to be limited under fiscally neutral policy. JPM FX strategists expect GBP to rally after the event, supported by positioning, with CFTC data showing GBP shorts near record levels.

JPM Research argues the current rates backdrop does not derail equities because earnings remain a strong anchor. It offers three baskets: Higher Rates (JPRHIRTB), Lower Rates (JPRLORTB) and Rate-Agnostic (JPRAGRTB).

JPM EM equity strategy says El Niño risk is still underpriced in EM. Index weights skew to low direct-exposure sectors, policy space is constrained by an energy-driven inflation shock, and agricultural effects can last four to five quarters past the peak.

El Niño effects differ by region. Latin America is mixed, with agricultural exporters benefiting from higher soft commodity prices and others facing drought and hydropower disruption. EM Asia (especially India and ASEAN) and Sub-Saharan Africa are more exposed through monsoon-driven food inflation.

Euro area ECB surveys (SAFE, Bank Lending Survey, September monetary aggregates) point to tighter bank lending conditions and weaker credit demand. Credit growth stayed resilient through September with no sign of acute stress, though the data does not capture the October stress in French yields.
APAC client sentiment is more bearish than in the US but less so than in the EU. Many APAC clients are up double digits on the year and lack incentive to re-engage until a clear trend emerges.

US consumer looks robust. The top four income quintiles hold 6% to 27% more inflation-adjusted cash than at YE2019 (nearly $8T nominal), retail sales are running at about $723bn a month YTD, and card delinquencies are normalizing to pre-COVID trends rather than deteriorating.
US corporates look healthy. HY default rates are 2.7% vs a 3.2% long-term average, after about 20% of HY market cap was upgraded to IG post-COVID.

Consumer sub-sector views from clients: airlines, cruise and hotels have robust demand. Autos and homebuilders face affordability problems so parts and suppliers may suit better. Retailers are hurt by freight costs. Restaurants lack conviction. Staples are most at risk of margin compression and likely a source of funds.

Credit markets are becoming more discriminating on AI infrastructure but there is no sign of a broader funding crisis. Hyperscalers are well positioned while leveraged GPU and data center developers face tighter financing.

AI infrastructure has absorbed more than $500 billion of debt YTD across IG, leveraged, structured and private credit. Hyperscaler all-in funding costs have risen by roughly 120bps. Power availability, rather than financing, is seen as the main constraint on expansion.

AI-related CDS spreads have widened mostly on technical selling and bank hedging of data center lending exposure rather than weaker fundamentals. CDS trading wider than cash bonds creates opportunities for bond investors willing to sell protection.

MSFT, GOOGL and AMZN credit remains resilient, while more externally financed names, particularly Oracle, have underperformed. ORCL and SpaceX spreads widened on reports each is seeking off-balance-sheet financing. JPM expects rising debt supply to pressure spreads into 2027.

JPM credit analyst Tom Egan sees CoreWeave (CRWV) as facing a financing challenge, not a solvency one. He projects last-12-month EBITDA rising from about $4.4b in June 2026 to $7.3b by year-end and nearly $20b by YE27, with about $130b of contracted revenue.

France contagion fears are called exaggerated. French debt/GDP is about 120% and the 180% threshold is 10 to 15 years away on unchanged policy. Greece, Italy and Spain have stronger fiscal profiles, and the ECB backstop (TPI, OMT, PEPP reinvestment) limits disorderly widening.

French bonds are priced for debt/GDP above 150% and an implied deficit above 8% vs about 5% debated. JPM does not call a material reversal before the 2Q27 elections but sees room for relief into year-end around the budget discussion.
EU banks: JPM sees the earnings trend as unchanged and says dips of more than 15% vs the index should be bought. Call ratio spreads and call spreads are attractive.

Midterms: AI regulation at the federal level is unlikely because Trump would veto and Democrats cannot reach a two-thirds majority. A Democratic House could defund Middle East military efforts. Tariff policy is unlikely to change, and longer-dated bonds could see a bid if Democrats curb deficit spending.

Treasuries: before the October 22 rally the view was that a 10-year yield of 5.50% was more likely than 5.00%. Markets price a hike in December 2026 and two in FY27. Clients see upside risk to that pricing. The downside risk is a quick end to the US/Iran conflict and normalizing oil, though that view is low conviction.

AI/tech pushback from clients: semi revenue is driven by supply-chain price spikes that are unsustainable in a DCF, neocloud turmoil could spread across the group, and software is no longer a funding source. Buying needs a positioning flush, hyperscaler capex confirmation, semis earnings and tighter credit, pointing to early November.

Market breadth is narrow. Since the July 28 lows the SPX is up 4.8% through Oct 22, but more than half the index has a negative return and 69% of stocks lag the SPX, which makes single-stock picks hedged with a sector ETF difficult.

An everything rally of AI and ex-AI together is viewed as possible short term but not longer term. About 65% of SPX companies cited AI operating improvement in 26Q2 earnings but fewer than 5% quantified it.

Cyclicals: clients focus on financials (GSIBs and credit cards). Industrials are seen as an AI play. Aero/defense has a negative outlook if a Blue Wave halts military funding, though a lame-duck defense funding bill could surprise higher.

To fund shorts against tech, clients suggested combining Consumer, Healthcare, small and mid caps and Europe. On other assets, most expect a range-bound dollar that has likely peaked locally, gold trading inversely to the dollar, no preference for credit over equities, a bullish copper view tied to China, and silver as part of the AI trade.

JPM Market Intelligence is tactically bullish on global equities, long US and Asia (Japan, South Korea, Taiwan) vs Europe. Broadening is more likely in the US than the EU, where EGB spread stability is needed first.

Longs: infrastructure, less-levered hyperscalers, AI-vulnerable application software, EU and JA banks, EU industrials, JA machinery, GE Infra, EU miners, EU pharma and UKX. Shorts: AI-vulnerable names ex-software, short-cycle data center capex names, EU insurance, autos, chemicals, Asian consumer electronics, MedTech and MDAX.

EM is bullish given global macro strength, AI capex tailwinds, commodity-driven broadening and policy easing scope. EM has recovered over 9% of its drawdown since the end-July bottom. Country-relative trades are preferred.

Positioning: hedge funds are -3.3% MTD globally vs SPX +0.2%, with alpha rather than beta driving the drawdown. CTAs were the most consistent sellers, retail buying slowed to the weakest pace in a year, and the move looks like systematic de-risking rather than a large liquidation.
Flows: relative flows into Info Tech are near record highs while Utilities, Real Estate and Materials flows are at or near extreme lows. Healthcare is the defensive exception.

Signs of stabilization include low crowding returns, slower multi-strat de-grossing, quants re-grossing and ETF dip buying. Risks are still-falling Eq L/S alpha, CTAs that could sell more, soft retail demand and gross leverage that has not fully cleared.

risk_factors: Growing AI debt issuance, interconnected financing arrangements and higher borrowing costs, with Nvidia a transmission channel for stress through GPU customers such as CRWV.
Leveraged GPU and data center developers face rising rates, possibly needing more equity, guarantees or revised deal structures.
French fiscal stress spreading to EU banks and sovereign spreads, worsened by crowded hedge fund carry positioning and a non-resident-heavy holder base.
US/Iran escalation after the midterms and an energy-driven inflation shock that constrains policy.
El Niño impacts on food inflation and rural demand in EM, with agricultural effects lasting four to five quarters.
Rate hikes priced by markets, with clients seeing upside risk to that pricing.
Narrow market breadth, with 69% of stocks lagging the SPX.
Further CTA and hedge fund de-risking while Eq L/S alpha is still deteriorating and retail demand is soft.
Semi revenue relying on supply-chain-driven price spikes that may be unsustainable.
Higher freight costs, which clients say have more than tripled YTD, pressuring retailers.
charts_described: Chart titled Drawdown in SOX vs SPX, which the text says rivals 2008 in size.
Table of 3-month returns after the war started in 2022, shown as a guide to what could work if geopolitics improve.
vol_and_positioning: Hedge funds are -3.3% MTD globally (from -2.1% the prior week) with SPX +0.2% MTD and ACWI -1.0%. YTD returns slipped to +4.7% from +6%.
Eq L/S 20d alpha of -2.9% is the worst since Feb 2021, and Multi-Strat alpha is the worst since Aug 2024. 60d crowding returns of -4.1% are back to July 2024 levels.
HF net flows were -0.9z (gross -0.6z). Multi-Strat 5d gross de-grossing slowed to -0.9% from -3.3% a week earlier, and Quants kept adding gross (80th percentile).

CTA US equity exposure has fallen every day since 10/13, led by Nasdaq, and sits only around the 45th percentile LT, so CTAs could still sell. Retail stayed net buyer at the slowest 20d pace in a year (5th percentile). ETFs bought, led by Tech.

Combined ETF, retail and HF 60d relative flows into Info Tech are near record highs (+3z vs +3.4z peak in late Sep). Utilities 60d -2.5z, Real Estate 20d -4.9z and Materials 60d -2.7z are at or near extreme lows. Healthcare 20d is +2.8z, HF-led.

US TPM is at the 28th percentile, Europe at the 8th and China/HK at -2z. Eq L/S net leverage is at 12-month and 3-year lows, but gross leverage is still at the 77th percentile (12m) and 95th (5yr) despite falling 4.4% WoW.
AI Core Revenue and Semis positioning fell to the 94th percentile LT from the 99th.
GBP shorts are near record levels in CFTC data ahead of the UK Budget.
geopolitical: Possible US vs Iran escalation after the US midterms, per WSJ headlines.
Russia vs Ukraine peace talks have revived.
Israeli elections projected to be inconclusive, with coalition dealmaking to follow.
France fiscal and political stress, with elections expected in 2Q27.
US midterms and the risk to Middle East military funding if Democrats take the House.
China Central Committee plenum starting in Beijing and the US-hosted G20 Foreign Ministers' Meeting on 10/30.

tension_points.bull_case: Hyperscalers are well positioned, banks retain lending capacity and AI CDS widening reflects technical selling and hedging rather than fundamentals. CRWV has about $130b of contracted revenue and a rising EBITDA path.
tension_points.bear_case: Debt issuance is growing, financing is interconnected, borrowing costs are up about 120bps and leveraged GPU and data center developers face tighter terms. Neocloud bankruptcy risk exists.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Clients want a positioning flush, hyperscaler capex confirmation, semis earnings and tighter credit before buying, pointing to early November.

tension_points.bull_case: Debt/GDP of about 120% is far from the 180% threshold, Italy, Spain and Greece have primary surpluses, the ECB backstop limits disorderly widening, and OATs over-discount fiscal risk.
tension_points.bear_case: France has a primary deficit near 3%, below-potential growth, crowded hedge fund carry positioning and a non-resident-heavy holder base. The EU bank tape echoes the 2011-12 sovereign crisis.
tension_points.what_invalidates: ECB backstop activation is conditional, and JPM does not call a material reversal before the 2Q27 elections.

tension_points.bull_case: Large cash piles, retail sales at $723bn a month YTD, normalizing delinquencies and healthy corporates.
tension_points.bear_case: Retail cost structure pressure from freight, trade-down in quick service restaurants, and rates-sensitive autos and homebuilders.

tension_points.bull_case: Strong household and corporate balance sheets, accelerating growth and inflation point to more hikes than priced.
tension_points.bear_case: A near-term end to the US/Iran conflict and quick normalization of oil, refined product, petrochemical and shipping costs would mean fewer hikes.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A near-term end to the US/Iran conflict followed by quick normalization of oil and shipping costs.
